# Wave vs Phasor: A Different Way to See Radio

When most people picture a radio wave, they imagine a familiar sine curve. Smooth, rhythmic, oscillating up and down.

![Simple sine wave illustration](images/sine_wave.png){#fig-sine fig-align="left" width=55%}

It's the classic visual taught in textbooks and classrooms. But there's another way to understand what's really going on.

Instead of thinking of the wave as something moving up and down, imagine it as the shadow of something rotating.

## From oscillation to rotation

Picture a simple arrow spinning in a circle, like a clock hand.

![Rotating phasor illustration](images/phasor.png){#fig-phasor fig-align="left" width=55%}

As it turns, imagine a light shining from one side, casting its shadow onto a flat surface. That shadow moves back and forth, tracing out the same sine wave shape we started with.

What looks like an oscillation is really just a projection of circular motion.

## The phasor

This rotating arrow has a name: a phasor. It's a rotating vector that represents a signal.

The concept is simple but changes how you think about signals. Instead of tracking amplitude over time directly, you can think in terms of rotation: angle, speed, and phase.

## The missing information problem

Here's where it gets interesting. If you only see the shadow (the sine wave), you can't tell which way the arrow is rotating. 

Imagine two arrows spinning in opposite directions. Their shadows look identical. From just the wave, you've lost information about the direction of rotation.

![Two counter-rotating phasors](images/counter_rotating.png){#fig-counter fig-align="left" width=55%}

This matters because a real radio wave can be thought of as two phasors rotating in opposite directions. The wave itself is the sum of both rotations.

## Adding a second shadow

What if we add another light source at 90 degrees to the first? Now we get two shadows: one horizontal, one vertical.

![Quadrature shadows](images/quadrature.png){#fig-quadrature fig-align="left" width=55%}

With both shadows, we can tell which way the arrow is rotating. The horizontal shadow is the cosine wave. The vertical shadow is the sine wave. Together, they define a single rotating phasor completely.

This is the foundation of I and Q.

## I and Q

The two shadows have names:

- I (In-phase): the cosine component
- Q (Quadrature): the sine component, 90 degrees shifted

Sine and cosine waves aren't just related mathematical functions. They're literally the horizontal and vertical projections of a single rotating phasor.

When you have both I and Q, you have complete information about the signal: its amplitude, phase, and frequency.

## Why this matters

Modern radios are increasingly software-defined radios (SDRs). They don't work with the wave directly. They work with I and Q samples.

Understanding phasors and why we need both I and Q is the key to understanding how modern radio actually works.

In the next post, we'll look at why SDRs use I and Q, and how radios actually generate these signals.
